summary: The Last Hope is an interactive space mission game for kids aged 7 to 12. It's the year 2089, Earth's water is contaminated, and the only antidote is on Mars. Players take the role of a father who gives everything to save his daughter and the world, so every choice feels personal. To answer the challenge, the game puts players in charge of a real mission. They manage limited resources under pressure the way astronauts do. Every decision affects what comes later. It’s a knowledge game, kids learn by doing. They apply the laws of physics and develop their critical thinking.
details:
The last hope is an interactive educational game designed for children aged 7–12. Set in 2089, Earth is facing a global water contamination crisis, and the only known antidote is believed to be on Mars. Players take on the role of Ethan, an astronaut, on a mission to find the antidote and save humanity.

The game takes players through different stages of a space mission, from preparing essential resources before launch to exploring Mars. They must manage CO₂ levels, fix spacecraft leaks, maintain orientation, navigate Mars orbit, deploy a robotic explorer, collect scientific data, and transmit the results back to Earth.

Through these challenges, children apply the laws of physics, develop critical-thinking and problem-solving skills, and learn about engineering, resource management, orbital mechanics, robotics, and space communication.

Technologies used:

  • HTML: Building the game's structure.
  • CSS: Designing the visual interface, animations, and overall aesthetic.
  • JavaScript: Developing the interactive elements, gameplay mechanics, and challenges.

The project's creativity comes from combining an emotional storyline with educational gameplay. Instead of simply reading about space science, children experience a space mission themselves, making decisions and solving challenges along the way.

During development, we considered the target age group, scientific accuracy, accessibility, visual engagement, educational value, and the limited development time of the 48-hour hackathon.
